subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN SEAL PELT QUOTA
speechtext:
The 1965 sealing season in the gulf area opened on March 8 with approximately 50 aircraft and five large sealing vessels licensed to operate in the area. A large concentration of seals was located about 15 to 20 miles east of North Point, P.E.I., and almost all the seal fishing is taking place in this patch.
The weather has been favourable during the early days of the season, and about 30,000 young seals were taken during the first three days. At this rate of catch it is expected that the total quota of 50,000 young seals will be taken very soon. There is no quota on older seals, that is on seals over one year old.
The quota of 50,000 young seals was established on the basis of scientific evidence gathered over the last 10 to 15 years which indicated that the gulf harp seal herds had been reduced to levels below that which would produce the maximum sustainable annual harvest. An established quota will permit a regular annual recovery of the herds to levels which will provide the maximum annual harvest.
Because of the favourable conditions which have permitted the fishermen to reach the quota during the first few days of the season, requests are now being received to extend the quota. I may say here, Mr. Speaker, that the regular season, which opened on Monday, was to close on April 26. After giving careful consideration to all the factors involved I have decided not to extend the quota for this season. Furthermore, just as I was coming to this chamber today word was received from our officers indicating that the quota would be taken by the end of operations today. Thus, fishing for young seals in the gulf by aircraft and licensed vessels will end today.

gram of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.

speechtext:
Order. Consideration of clauses 69, 71, 78, 79, 91 and 110 will be the next business of the committee. When we adjourned yesterday the committee had reached consideration of clause 69.
On clause 69-Monthly exempt earnings defined.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking to this clause I do so in a spirit of cooperation, and I hope I may receive the same treatment from the ministers involved in this particular bill. I feel that the bill is of such very serious importance to everyone living in our country that it is only by co-operation with regard to some of its clauses which I think could be improved that we can hope to come out with a pension bill that will be reasonably acceptable to the people.
This particular clause, of course, is phrased in technical language which it is difficult for an ordinary person to understand. However, I am given to understand, and my understanding is confirmed by the white paper, that it simply means that anyone between 65 and 70-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Order. I apologize for interrupting the hon. gentleman. There is a little too much noise in the chamber and it is difficult to hear the hon. member who is now commenting on clause 69. Maybe the usual courtesy could be extended to the hon. member.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. It is not easy for me to speak at any time, and certainly it is more difficult when there is noise. The point is that if you break down the clause into ordinary language it simply means that if a person reaches the age of 65 and continues to have any income over $900 a year, then no matter how long he has paid into the pension plan, whether for 47 years or less, from $900 to $1,500 some 50 per cent of such earnings are deducted from his pension, and over $1,500 there is a 100 per cent deduction from his pension. This in itself is a very serious matter, but there are other serious implications as well as the financial one, and I believe we should give this clause considerable thought.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he said on February 25 that in the booming economy we are ex-

periencing in this country we are completely wrong even to give a thought to the idea that $200 a month will be a lot of money in the future. I agree with him that we should consider $200 a month a very niggardly amount. I bring out that fact only because when he mentioned it the other day it confirmed my impression with regard to this particular clause. As he stated, it is a starvation wage, and we should not think of these figures as being adequate at all for future generations. In my opinion this particular clause is based completely on the economic viewpoint, and the economic viewpoint is not the most important implication in the clause but rather the least important.
Before I go on to what I consider to be the serious shortcomings of the clause I should like us to ask ourselves one or two questions. What happens to those people who have contributed to the plan for all these years when they reach the age of 65? Think of the farmer. He probably has not made a great amount of money and has to continue operating his farm because the income from his pension is not sufficient. Is he supposed to give up his farm? What about the small storekeeper or small businessman? Is he supposed to close his doors so he can get his $104 a month from the pension plan?
To me these are serious matters. What about tradesmen? Let us say a man is a carpenter and wishes to do a little carpentry work after he is 65. If he does and makes any reasonable return, it is deducted from his pension and he gets no pension until he is 70. The same thing applies to all other occupations. If one of our friends in the press gallery decides when he reaches the age of 65 that he is going to write a column for a newspaper he will find himself with no pension, even though he has been paying into the fund for many years. If he decides to write a book on the peculiarities of the people he looks down on from the gallery he will find he has no income from the pension plan. These are purely economic features.
With all due respect, I find that in the bill the Minister of National Health and Welfare is creating a paradoxical situation.
She is riding two horses, one the economic horse and the other the health and welfare horse. They are going in different directions, and if that situation continues we are going to get into serious trouble.
We have in the world today, and we are certainly not exempt from it in Canada, a very serious medical problem that arises in con-
Canada Pension Plan
nection with people who are 65 years of age and over. These people, who have been mentally and physically active all their lives, find they are pensioned off at 65. They are put out to pasture. What happens? They deteriorate physically and mentally; then we have what we call a geriatrics problem. Now, Mr. Chairman, I feel this is one of the serious results of this clause. We are putting these people in the position where they have to discontinue their work at a time when they should be engaged in some part time activity. If these people could be encouraged to carry on some form of mental and physical activity they would be very much less of a burden on the welfare of our country.
I say, therefore, that this is a problem the minister faces. She is basing this bill on an economic principle. I am afraid this is going to lead eventually not to an economic saving in the country but an economic loss. I do not believe we can really look at the problems of the health and welfare of our people from a purely economic aspect.
What will happen if we keep on with this particular type of plan? It will simply mean those people who are going to retire at 65, such as the farmer and businessman, will have to sell their farm or close down their business. This will mean we will have to have more homes for the aged, more hospitals, more nursing homes and more mental institutions. Hon. members may feel that I am exaggerating the situation. I am sincere when I say this problem of geriatrics is a serious problem for our country. I feel that this particular clause will simply increase the problem of looking after these elderly people who reach 65 years of age. I feel we should not deprive these people of their initiative. We should encourage them to have some mental and physical activity.
I should like to ask the minister if she would give some consideration to the health and welfare of our senior citizens. Will she give some consideration to the comfort and happiness of our senior citizens? Will she give some consideration to the long term economic situation that will develop from the increased unemployment that we are going to create amongst these older citizens? Personally I would eliminate this clause. I am only trying to compromise when I advance this suggestion. I say that in the interests of our elderly citizens this clause should be completely eliminated; let there be no misunderstanding about that.
Since it is quite likely, however, that this clause will remain, I should like to ask the

Canada Pension Plan
minister to please give some consideration to modifying, in line 3, page 52, the figure 1.5 per cent to 3 per cent. This will not allow anyone to have a large income, but at least it should help to encourage activity amongst our senior citizens. I should like to know whether the minister is prepared to give this suggestion consideration. If she is I will leave the matter at that point; otherwise I should like to speak further on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand my hon. friend's concern with the problem of geriatrics. I hope he will appreciate that the department of health and welfare, being a dual department, during the last few years has spent an increasing amount of its time on this very problem, as indeed other public bodies have. The hon. member knows that for the last two years there has been a Senate committee dealing wth the problems of aging. It must be quite obvious to my hon. friend that the department, in preparing the Canada pension plan, had to take a very wide view of those approaching retirement age and the effects this retirement plan would have on our national labour policies, as well as what it would mean to the health of our older citizens and what it would mean with regard to recreation. Almost every aspect had to be considered.
I think my hon. friend, being a doctor, is particularly aware of the interest that not only the department of welfare but the department of health have had in this field. In essence what my hon. friend is asking is the removal of what we call the retirement test for those who take their wage related pension at age 65. I think we should be very clear about the fact, first, that no one is forced to take this portion of his pension at 65. If I may, for a moment, assume that the committee will adopt the part IV amendments which are proposed by the Prime Minister, then this will mean that every human being in this country, provided he meets the residence test, when he reaches the age of 65 is going to have available to him a pension without any means test of $900. You cannot forget this. There is no point in talking in a vacuum, and we must not forget that there are two halves of the program the government has designed for people who retire in this country.
With respect to the wage related part again, I should like to underline the fact that no one who is age 65 need take his or her pension. It is a matter of application. The individual, when approaching the age of 65, will have to look at what his pension would

be. He will have to consider his own circumstances. If a man of 65 who lives on a farm does not wish to stop farming, he does not have to sell his farm. Remember, this is true only of earned income, and he is able to have investment income. So long as his earned income does not go above a certain level, then his contributory pension is not reduced in any way. If he wishes to go on farming there is no reason why he should not do so as long as his health and his own inclination is that way. I would expect that many active, vigorous people approaching the age of 65 may feel they would rather work. If this happens they can go ahead and work and earn whatever income they can, and I would hope it would be a very adequate income.
Many hon. members opposite were talking earlier about the drop out years. If a man continued working beyond 65 he would have an opportunity to catch up on those drop out years because of bad crops or other reasons. If he is in full, vigorous health and wants to work and can make a good income, he can draw his $900 from old age security and go ahead and make all the income he can, subject of course to the income tax provisions which are applicable to everyone in the country, and put in one of those good years for the years in which he had a bad crop, was ill or had dropped out for some other reason. In this way he can make sure that when he does retire his wage related pension is going to be higher.
I think my hon. friend should realize that in the closest comparable schemes, which are those of the U.K. and the U.S., there is also the same kind of retirement test. We do not want to pay pensions to people who are members of the labour force, but in this particular case when the man retires-or when he reaches the age of 70-then he has a higher pension because of having worked on beyond the age of 65 at top earnings, of which the maximum is now $5,000 a year and perhaps it will be more in the future.
All this time he has the additional $900 a year which he does not have to retire in order to obtain, and this means that when he does retire he will have almost $2,400. If he decides to take his pension and keeps on doing some work he can have over $3,000. There is the allowance of $900, under clause 69, as well as the $900 he gets because he has resided in Canada for the required period, and at the age of 65 years or over he is going to be able to draw this much, almost $50 a week together with his pension of up to $1,250.

I suggest to my hon. friend that the things he proposes would lead to pressure on older people to stay at work. I do not know whether he was present when many members of the house and of the cabinet heard the very long and very good presentation made by the Canadian Labour Congress. It is not too difficult to see that over the years there will be more and more pressure to reduce the age for retirement; and remember, the Canada pension plan is a projection for a great many years, probably forever.
My hon. friend has also heard those in the Creditiste corner saying there ought to be a flat rate pension payable at age 60. There are many people, and I might personally subscribe to this, who think we ought to pay a pension to women at age 60 or 62. Many countries in the world make such provision and allow for such differences between men and women who are part of the labour force, but it all has to be balanced against the question of increasing productivity, against the fact that a man or woman can produce much more than they could 20 years ago. The whole labour policy has to be covered to keep men working to age 70 for their own individual good, and from his own practice I am sure my hon. friend will agree it is a real hardship to keep people working beyond age 65. You have to balance this against the increasing productivity and low demand for labour, especially older labour.
Physical labourers who approach age 65 find it increasingly difficult to keep up their end, whether it be on the farm or in the factory, and I dare say that in the next few years there will be more and more pressure to lower the age for those who rely on physical dexterity or strength, so they will have to retire at an earlier age.
We balanced all this very seriously. This was one of the reasons the Prime Minister announced that he would introduce, with the part IV amendments, a provision which would give individuals the present basic old age security allowance at age 65. It is up to those 65 and over to decide whether to apply to take the contributory pension they are entitled to then or to defer it for a few years, possibly until the age of 70.
We have done everything we could to get flexibility, to fit within the changing circumstances in the labour market and the problem of what to do with people you push off the labour market and sort of condemn to die, as it were, because they have nothing useful to do. I think the committee will agree that, having considered all the problems, we ar-
Canada Pension Plan
rived at a good balance in giving one flat rate pension with no retirement test, and another earnings related one with a retirement test. As I have pointed out, both the U.S. and U.K. contributory schemes have such tests.
Further, the $25 flat rate benefit in the amendment proposed by the Progressive Conservative party was to have been subject to a retirement test, and the Ontario government, which considered the plan for some considerable length of time, also favoured a retirement test, and even suggested a retirement test which should be extended beyond the wage related part of the plan to old age security.
Over the past two years we have considered this problem in depth and it is the government's decision, based on the balance of factors involved, that the proposal embodied in clause 69 is the one which will best meet the needs not only of today but of people who approach the age of 65 and then decide at that late point whether they want to go on earning or retire and have the fruits of their pension at that date.

speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, the subject that has been opened up by the hon. member for Kamloops is a very important one, and I think all of us will agree that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has given an indication of the fact that a great deal of attention has been given to this question. I believe the hon. member for Kamloops makes a good point when he suggests that times are changing; that we are gaining new attitudes with respect to the position of older people. Therefore I would like to hear some pretty serious discussion on the amendment which the hon. member has proposed.
I may say that I followed this subject very closely when we were in the special joint committee, and as the record will show- there being no doubt about it-I made no complaint about the retirement test with respect to the Canada pension plan benefits. Members of the committee will recall that my major concern, when we were in the special joint committee, with regard to persons between 65 and 70 was that they might be given the old age security pension and that it might be in the amount of $100. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I would like to put this question to the minister. Has any revised thinking been done about this question since the government made the decision to reduce the eligible age for old age security to 65? For the moment I am not arguing about the fact that it is going to take us five years to get down to that age; the fact is that the principle has been accepted that old age security is going to be paid in full at age 65. Does that not suggest that the government has accepted some of the new thinking about people in that age bracket?
I notice that in the record of the committee, when we were discussing this matter-the record is found on page 324, 325 and so on of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence for Tuesday, December 8-Mr. Thorson and Dr. Willard were giving the answers and most of the questions were being asked by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. At one point the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich asked this question:
Does his initial figure of $900 relate to something, or was it taken out of thin air?

The answer by Mr. Thorson was:
It is arrived at by reference to the year's maximum pensionable earnings. However, I do not think that is the answer you are looking for. Perhaps Doctor Willard could answer your question.
Our staff learned something from us, namely how to pass a question from one to another. Dr. Willard's reply was this:
In arriving at these levels, account was taken of the old age security benefit.
The rest of the answer was this:
We did get to levels that would assure a reasonable level of pensionable and other income when the two were taken together.
The point I am making-and the basis of my question is in this point-is that when the $900 and $1,500 figures were arrived at, the points at which the pension benefit is cut back if you are making income after age 65, the government had in mind old age security benefits at a reduced level. I know the government can say, "We have now increased that amount, so does that not move us in the other direction?" But I am looking at this change regarding old age security as a change in principle, as accepting the fact that people aged 65 should not be discriminated against as compared with other older people. I wonder whether any new thinking has been done about the amount at which people should be considered retired, in relation to the new stand being taken regarding old age security.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I might take the liberty of explaining what I understand the amendment of the hon. member for Kamloops to mean. When he changes the figure 1.5 per cent that appears in the bill to the figure of 3 per cent, the result would be, under today's $5,000 contributory earnings ceiling, that instead of $900 being the point at which the pension benefit would be cut back by 50 per cent, that point would be $1,800.

Likewise, instead of $1,500 being the point at which it would be cut back by 100 per cent, that point would not be reached until $3,000. I say quite readily to my hon. friend from Kamloops that, though I liked the philosophical approach he was making earlier, I was not happy about his suggestion that the clause be wiped out altogether. It seems to me there are actuarial and other considerations to be taken into account. In my view his amendment-I know this may sound strange coming from me-is more responsible than his proposal to wipe
Canada Pension Plan
the clause out altogether. This proposal that the cut-off point should be changed from $900 and $1,500 to $1,800 and $3,000 respectively is a serious one on which we should have some comment by both ministers, perhaps after they have had a chance to consult their advisers. I have not done all the arithmetic I could have wished, but I should like to see this amendment put in terms of what can be the total income of people between 65 and 70, taking into account their earned income, income from old age security, and so on. This is the sort of amendment which ought to be given serious consideration by the minister.
There is just one point on which the minister commented with which I agree. I think she was trying to make the point that people between 65 and 70 cannot expect to have it both ways. In other words, they cannot both draw the pension and get credit on their earnings to improve their pension later on. I agree that either they draw the pension under the Canada pension plan or keep on working to improve their pension at a later period, but they should not have both. But if they do decide to draw the pension, in the light of our newer thinking about people in the 65 to 70 bracket I am wondering whether there should not be a further statement from the minister as to the amendment. Her earlier statement on the suggestion that the clause should be wiped out altogether was quite impressive and I think she persuaded me not to vote for the elimination of the clause altogether, but I should like to hear what she says about the amendment, for it strikes me as one we should support.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Obviously the government did consider this when it first drew up the Canada pension plan. It provided a pension at 65, and in doing so the government acknowledged this principle for the first time in the history of parliament. But in reconsidering the matter over a period of time it was appreciated that what would happen would be that people who took the pension at 65 would have a smaller pension, which is why the government decided that the O.A.S. amendment which will be proposed to part IV of the bill will provide that people can draw the full $75 pension at age 65. Of course at that time the government considered whether or not there should be some change one way or the other in the limits of permissible income under clause 69; but as my hon. friend will appreciate, what this proposed amendment does is to increase the amount in the hands of an individual at 65, which increase is not taken into account when it comes to esti-
mating his income. Accordingly there is even less reason to touch the amount up to age 69; if there is any reason at all it would be to downgrade the amount instead of to double it, as my hon. friend from Kamloops is doing.
It seems to me that when you compare pension legislation in other parts of the world with the circumstances in this country, fairly generous sums are being allowed which will permit a man and his wife to earn a substantial sum of money without having their pensions touched, which is something which no Canadian need blush about when you compare his pension with those offered in other countries. Indeed, this clause of the act, as many others, is something which the Canadian people can take some pride in. I would suggest to my hon. friend and the committee that there is really not a great deal more we can dispute about this matter and perhaps it is time for the committee to divide on this clause.

That is exactly the situation I had in mind when I asked the question. We are sitting here passing laws, we are not attempting to provide jobs for every lawyer across Canada. Surely we must make our laws abundantly clear and understandable so that everyone who wishes to find out the position he is in will not have to go to a lawyer for an interpretation. Let us have a clearcut understanding of the provisions of this bill.
The crop sharing arrangement I have referred to is something that takes place all across Canada, not only in Alberta or in western Canada. Many farmers who retire because of ill health, or for other reasons, turn their farms over to sons or neighbours on a crop sharing basis. That is a very reasonable, understandable and ordinary proposition carried out time and time again in Canada. Before this amendment is agreed to I should like the minister to give us a clear explanation as to its effect. It is now that we must make these things abundantly clear. We do not wish to provide extra jobs for lawyers all across Canada. The Lord knows that they have enough jobs as things are at the present time, because we all run into difficulty and have to consult them. Let us have a clear understanding of this amendment and this clause.
Will the income a retired farmer receives from a crop sharing arrangement be investment income? It is normal for a retired farmer to make such an arrangement so that in the event of a crop failure the individual

Canada Pension Plan
operating the farm will not have to meet exorbitant rentals, whereas in normal crop years both he and the retired farmer will do well. Surely the income that a man receives on that basis should be considered as investment income.
Mr. Chairman, I am not asking the minister to give us any legal opinions. If this bill was law at this time and I asked the minister to give me a definition in respect of a particular clause, then I would expect him to stand in his place and say he is not in a position to make a legal judgment. Mr. Chairman, subclause (2) of clause 43 provides for the definition of disability and for matters connected with its determination and for the making of certain regulations. After a careful examination of the provisions in the bill, the joint committee made recommendations respecting a number of matters which it felt should be more precisely dealt with by regulation. The purpose of the amendment to clause 91 is therefore to give full effect to these important recommendations of the committee by adding two new subclauses to clause 91 to set these matters out in greater detail.
Although hon. members have before them the recommendations of the committee in both languages, dated February 15, I might say a few words of additional explanation as to the main areas which would be covered by this provision.
An applicant in respect of whom a disability benefit is claimed will be required in the first instance to provide at his own expense the initial report from his physician on the basis of which a determination might be made or further evidence required. If further evidence is required by way of assessment of the individual's condition the cost of this, as I explained some days ago, will be borne not by the applicant but out of the fund. It is considered that the applicant should be responsible for the cost of other than the initial evidence which he should be able to obtain through his own family doctor.
I should also like to say that we would be prepared to give reasonable assistance to an applicant in respect to his initial application where this was required in his interest.
In a number of cases it may be considered that the individual's disability can be reduced and his working capacity improved through suitable rehabilitation procedures. It would

be considered entirely in the interest of the individual that he take advantage of these measures where they are practicable and available. Clearly, he should not be penalized by way of loss of benefit while undergoing recommended treatment or vocational training measures. It might also happen that as part of his therapy he should engage in some form of therapeutic or trial employment for a sufficient period to reach a conclusion as to his ability to engage in gainful employment. This, where recommended, he would be able to do without loss of benefit.
Every encouragement would therefore be given to individuals to take advantage of such measures as might be practicable and available to them to ameliorate or assist in overcoming their disability. Regulations in this connection would be made and the payment of the cost of assessments, as well as rehabilitation, would, under the amendment, be borne under the plan.
It would be logical that even where a determination of disability had been made and a benefit was being paid, there should be continued proof of the disability in question. The regulations would provide for not only the initial assessment but for periodic and other assessments as from time to time would seem desirable. Here again the cost of these assessments would be borne by the plan. While all of the disability procedures have not yet been worked out, it would be contemplated that full utilization would be made of all remedial and other facilities that are available to improve the individual's vocational capacities. While every opportunity and encouragement will be given to persons to take full advantage of rehabilitation as available and recommended, undoubtedly cases will arise where persons for one reason or another will refuse to do so. The committee therefore proposed that where rehabilitation is recommended, failure to undergo rehabilitation without "good cause" should be a ground for a determination that such person had ceased to be disabled for the purposes of the act.
Subsection (f), as is proposed, is designed to take care of this type of situation. Regulations would be made to cover the circumstances as contemplated by the committee and as might from time to time be found necessary. Hon. members can be assured that regulations would take full account of justifiable reasons by an individual for refusing to undergo reasonable rehabilitation measures. For example, surgical or other procedures, where there may be some risk of damage to
Canada Pension Plan
the individual, would clearly constitute good cause. Another ground that might be considered in due course would be whether refusal based on religious belief should constitute good cause. The government has received representations from the Christian Scientists asking that this be done as in the United States. Assurance was given that this would be carefully considered. What I have said is not, of course, exhaustive of all matters that might constitute good cause, but illustrates the type of refusal that would be considered.
This concludes what I thought might be helpful in explanation of the committee's valuable recommendations which are reflected in the amendments that are before you. It is felt that regulations of the kind mentioned will permit of a desirable degree of flexibility in the determination of disability, the conditions under which benefits can be paid and continue to be paid, the circumstances where rehabilitative and other measures may usefully be engaged in, as well as matters of cost. All these matters are in the interests of the individuals concerned and have full regard to their pension entitlement and welfare.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is moved by my colleague the Minister of National Revenue:
That subsection (1) of section 91 be amended by renumbering paragraphs (e) to (i) as paragraphs (g) to (k), respectively, and by adding immediately after paragraph (d) the following paragraphs:
"(e) respecting the determination of disability subject to this part, and the conditions upon which any amount as or on account of a benefit in respect of the disability of a person shall be paid or shall continue to be paid, including the initial and subsequent periodic or other assessments of such disability and the reasonable rehabilitation measures to be undergone by such person, and providing for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of the cost of any such assessments of disability and rehabilitation measures and for the charging of the amount thereof to the Canada pension plan account as a cost of administration of this act;
(f) providing that the failure of a person to undergo any assessment of disability or reasonable rehabilitation measure as required by any regulation made under paragraph (e), without good cause as defined by regulation, shall be a ground on which that person may be determined to have ceased to be disabled;"

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. S-36, to incorporate Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada-Miss	Jewett-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the present widespread and practical interest in higher education has been expressed in many ways. One of the most obvious ways has been the co-operative efforts of the universities themselves through two organizations, the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges and the Canadian universities foundation. This bill simply brings together these two bodies into a single organization for greater efficiency. It is a tidying up process. This organization will serve two purposes. It will serve as an agency for the distribution of federal grants to universities, and it will provide a medium through which universities and colleges can communicate and cooperate in advancing the interests of higher education. We are pleased to support the bill.
Private Bills

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I only wish to direct a question to the hon. member who acts as sponsor of this bill.
Can the hon. member tell us whether, as incorporated, the association of universities and colleges of Canada will be in a position to ask for federal grants to assist universities and colleges?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this association will operate in this respect in the same way that the association it replaces operated. That is to say, it will act to some extent as the liaison between the universities and the government wherever such liaison is necessary. It will act as spokesman for the universities on whatever matters the universities require a spokesman vis-a-vis the government. If that includes financial matters I assume it will speak on those matters as well as others.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that is not quite an answer to the question I asked.
Will one of the objects of this association of universities and colleges of Canada be to obtain federal grants for the association members, that is the colleges and universities belonging to it?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: It will distribute federal grants just as the Canadian universities foundation does now.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, today the Canadian universities and classical colleges foundation gets its grants through the Canada Council.
Will the new association have the privilege to get directly from the federal government grants that it would hand over afterwards to colleges and universities?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
My understanding is that the Canadian universities foundation now distributes what it calls the per capita grants. It is the agency in this country for the distribution of these grants. Under the new legislation the new association will take over that function. It will not have any additional function. In other words, there will not be, unless the parliament of this country so desires, any other grants to be distributed through this new association, apart from the per capita grants which are already distributed through its predecessor.

Private Bills

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the present time, the Canadian universities and colleges foundation distributes subsidies to the amount of $1.50 or $2 per capita to universities, but only to the universities in the nine English provinces in Canada, and not to those of the province of Quebec.
Under Bill No. S-36, will the association of universities and colleges of Canada hold special privileges to do the same in the province of Quebec as the foundation did in the other provinces?
On the other hand, will the provincial privileges not be infringed upon through the incorporation of the association of universities and colleges of Canada?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member can rest assured that the arrangement whereby the per capita grants are distributed to universities in the province of Quebec, in a way which is different from the way they are distributed in the rest of the country, will remain unchanged. As the hon. member knows, the per capita grants are now distributed to all universities in Canada, except those in the province of Quebec, through the Canadian universities foundation, and they will continue to be so distributed. Under the new legislation the distribution of these grants to the universities in the province of Quebec will continue in exactly the same way as they have been distributed since 1960.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, one last question. Will the federal government give any other subsidies or grants whatsoever to the association of universities and colleges of Canada, which will allocate them to the universities and colleges of the province of Quebec? Can the hon. member give us any assurance in that respect?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, unless the parliament of Canada decided that there should be further grants, what the hon. gentleman says is quite correct.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Could the parliament of Canada then decide to grant subsidies to the association of universities and colleges of Canada so that they might revert to Quebec colleges and universities?
I feel that if this new piece of legislation enabled the federal government to pass

through a new corporation in order to distribute subsidies to colleges and universities, this would constitute a serious breach of the privileges granted to the province of Quebec under section 93 of the British North America Act. That is why we would object to it; but if the hon. member can assure us that this association will not be used to infringe upon the rights of the provinces in the field of education, we shall allow Bill No. S-36 to be passed. If, however, the federal government took the liberty, through this new association or corporation, to distribute subsidies to Quebec colleges and universities, we would like the hon. member to say so, because then we would raise strong objections.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this association is made up of all the universities and colleges in Canada, including French speaking universities and colleges, which are eligible, and I am quite sure that these institutions, whether English or French speaking, would be the last ones to do anything which would in any way take away from the legitimate and rightful powers of government, even if they were capable of doing so. For that reason I believe the hon. member is expressing a fear about a body which, in my view at any rate, is quite able itself to look after the kind of problem he raises. Since I have already stated that there is no additional power being granted by this legislation to this association, the hon. member can rest assured that the problems he has referred to are not substantial ones.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into the much broader question of provincial rights, or the interpretation which some members would make as to whether or not provincial rights are being encroached upon or invaded, but it has always seemed very strange to me that in respect of one province it is perfectly acceptable in principle or in theory to make grants directly or indirectly from the federal treasury to universities or through the predecessor of this organization which we are about to incorporate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. member that he is now embarking upon a field of discussion that is far beyond the very limited confines of clause 1 of this bill. It does not seem to me that this is the time to discuss the very large problem which he appears to be talking about, or attacking at this point.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
I do not intend to do that, Mr. Chairman, but having listened to the questions asked by the hon. member for Lapointe and the answers he received, it seemed to me that they touched upon that which the hon. member for Lapointe considers to be the rights of a provincial government, specifically Quebec, under the constitution. There was some expression to the effect that this particular association of universities and colleges of Canada would not encroach upon those rights. That is an extremely broad subject which goes beyond the bill; however, it is something that we must consider.
I do not wish to get into that subject matter, Mr. Chairman, but it has always seemed strange to me that we should be called upon to take two different attitudes, one which applies to one province and another which applies to another province. That is precisely what we are being asked to do. It seems to me that when we are enacting laws in this parliament of Canada we should do so with the knowledge that there will be universal application rather than-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Order, please. I have reread clause 1 of this bill but I cannot see that the comments which are now being made by the hon. member are relevant. I appreciate that some reference was made by the hon. member for Lapointe to the subject now being discussed by the hon. member for Skeena, but the hon. member for Lapointe asked specific questions, one of which was related to the consequences of the passage of this bill, and whether they would affect the relationship between the federal and provincial governments on matters of education. The answer to that question was that they would not have that effect. I suggest that answer ends the discussion in respect of that problem. If the hon. member for Skeena continues along the lines he has been following it is my opinion he will be going beyond the terms of the bill, and certainly beyond the terms of this specific clause.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
With your guidance, Mr. Chairman, it might be that I should properly raise this matter during our consideration of a subsequent clause, namely clause 8 which deals with the powers of the association. Clause 8 (e) deals with powers to take, receive, accept or acquire property, rights or money, personal or real, movable or immovable. Presumably this association will have the power to distribute that money. Perhaps I should raise my question as to what the 20220-7751

association will do with the money it receives from this parliament in respect of that clause. If I was in error in raising this question on clause 1 I certainly apologize, but I felt that because the hon. member for Lapointe got into a discussion in this regard, although in a small way, I would be able to do the same.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like you, I do not really see the relevance of the hon. member's argument to any clause of the bill, in fact.
Perhaps I may be allowed to make a few remarks to clarify one statement which has been made. The hon. member seems to feel that this association will have at its discretion certain powers in relation to giving certain amounts of federal money to universities of Canada. The association will not have such a discretionary power.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Excuse me, Mr. Chairman, but it has such powers.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: If the parliament of Canada decides that the association shall continue to be the distributing agency of per capita grants in certain provinces, as it has decided, that will be the case. If the parliament of Canada also decides that there shall be some other method of distributing these per capita grants in the province of Quebec, as it has decided, all this association will be able to do is carry out that will of parliament. What the hon. member is suggesting, Mr. Chairman, is that we consider this whole large and very important area in respect of how per capita grants should be and are being distributed. Surely that is not relevant to this bill, which is designed to set up the association. This association does not have the discretionary freedom to decide how these funds are to be distributed.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether you will be courteous enough to permit me to ask, out of ignorance, what enactment or authority exists which limits the control or restricts the powers of the association to distribute moneys received from the parliament of Canada.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: This is done by the parliament of Canada itself.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
If I understood the hon. member correctly, he was asking who decides whether the grant is to be $2 per capita or otherwise. That is done by the parliament of

Canada. The parliament of Canada also decides how this money is to be distributed.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Oh, no.

Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Order, please. Will the hon. member for Lapointe kindly resume his seat. Only one person can be standing at any one time. Perhaps that suggestion might come from the hon. member for Lapointe at this stage, but it is obvious now that we are getting involved in a discussion which to my mind, and I have to rule accordingly, is not within the confines of Bill No. S-36. Clause 1 deals with the incorporation of the association of universities and colleges of Canada, and nowhere in the bill, not even in clause 8, is there any reference to the distribution of the per capita grants and the amounts of grants given by the federal government for education purposes. maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will not argue the point with you at this stage but it is my submission that when we get to clause 2, which is more pertinent, we will have a valid argument because clause 2 states that the objects of the association shall be to foster and promote the interests of higher education in Canada. I submit that those objects cannot be met if there are restrictions upon the manner in which the association will operate, albeit those restrictions are made by some other statute.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: This might be a very good argument on clause 2 but we are on clause 1 at this stage and the Chair should not be asked to rule in anticipation.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: I am just giving notice.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
I wish to speak on clause 1, Mr. Chairman.
If, as the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) has just claimed, the federal government has the required authority to

decide which contributions or subscriptions to universities will be made through the association of universities and colleges of Canada, then the corporation which is being set up becomes in fact an organization which will have the necessary powers to evade the provisions of the British North America Act.
As the hon. member for Northumberland has just mentioned, the federal government will be able to use this organization after incorporating it, in order to decide which subsidies it will grant, in which amounts and to whom and how they will be distributed. If those are the purposes of this bill, it cannot be accepted, because we claim that it is not a responsibility of the federal government to determine

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member commenting on the point of order which has been raised?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I am speaking on clause 1.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Well, in that case, the statement of the hon. member is out of order because it is related to a point which does not come in the ambit of clause 1. It may be that the argument of the hon. member could be set forth on another clause, later, but as far as the discussion on this clause is concerned, I consider, as I have already suggested to the hon. members, that we should adhere strictly to its content.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, could the hon. member for Northumberland tell me why the federal government should grant a corporate charter to the association of universities and colleges of Canada when those universities and colleges come under education, a field which is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces according to the British North America Act.
I have nothing against the granting of a federal charter to Canadian universities and colleges but, on the other hand, I would not want this charter granted to Canadian universities and colleges to be used in order to bypass the purposes of section 92 of the British North America Act.
Following the answer just given by the hon. member for Northumberland, to the effect that the federal government is authorized to do this, I wonder if the granting of such a federal charter is not precisely for the purpose of evading the provisions of section 93 of the British North America Act.
When she says that the federal government is authorized to make such grants, I would

like her to explain clearly how those grants would be distributed, what would be their amounts and, also, whether some areas are implied or whether provincial jurisdiction is being encroached upon.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps I might make two brief comments. First of all, the function of the association is only in part to act as an agent for the federal government in the distributing of grants. It has a great many other functions of great importance that we will come to, no doubt, under clause 2. It acts as agent of the federal government for the distribution of per capita grants, just as the Canadian universities foundation has acted for many years at the request of the federal government.
As I said earlier, I am sure the association has no desire to do anything other than what is within the law. If the federal parliament of Canada has determined that the payment of per capita grants is within its spending power, and this has not been challenged elsewhere in the courts-

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: With the consent of the provinces.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: -if this has been determined by the parliament of Canada and has not been challenged, as indeed it has not, by the courts or elsewhere, then surely it is not up to us here to decide whether or not at this particular point the per capita grant concept is one which should or should not continue. All we need to do here, if I may say so, is to assist an association which has requested incorporation to perform its multitudinous tasks, only one of which is to act as an agent for the federal government in the pursuit of a policy which is legal, which is in fact constitutional and which has not in fact been challenged.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: It has been done with the consent of the provinces, but it is not according to the constitution.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not very often that I share the views of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), but I feel that he has just raised a very interesting point which is closely related to the very principle of provincial autonomy in the field of public education.
After listening to the remarks made by the mover of the bill, I have the impression that the main purpose of this measure is to enable the association to be the federal gov-
Private Bills
ernment's agent, in the field of education, to distribute grants to the provinces' universities. Therefore, it is a hypocritical bill through which the federal government creates an association whose primary purpose will be to interfere in the field of education, which is the provinces' exclusive responsibility.
I see nothing wrong in the various classical colleges and universities of the province being incorporated. But when the sponsor of the bill tells us that the main purpose of that association will be to act as trustee, spokesman, agent, treasurer or distributor of federal grants in the field of education, then I respectfully submit that the Canadian constitution is being violated.
For my part, I shall not support this measure until we know what the aims of the association are. Besides, we should be told whether this is a free association of universities and colleges or if the universities and colleges have been asked by the federal government to form a corporation so the government can intrude in an area where it does not belong.
In my opinion, this would be the first step toward the creation of a federal department of education, because unfortunately that is what too many in this house want.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I will stand against the passing of this bill because it infringes upon the provinces' exclusive jurisdiction in the field of education.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a question to the sponsor of the bill. Will the members of that association or corporation draw salaries from the government grants, or will their work be unpaid? In my opinion, it is important to know whether they work as a voluntary body or whether they are paid by the government, in order to know their interest in their work?

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: So far as I am aware, Mr. Chairman, and I would have to check this, there is no other fee paid for the small service they perform. In so far as the prior question is concerned, member institutions are not in any way paid by the government. This is purely a voluntary body financed by a levy on its own members.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether at this stage, the hon. member for Northumberland does not feel it would be in order to make a statement concerning federal grants to the corporation or association
122S2

Private Bills
of universities and colleges of Canada, because the matter is obscure and we would like to know what to think.
I think that as long as this matter is not clarified, it will be difficult for us to take a stand.
In view of the fact that we know very little about it at the present time and in view of the statement made by my colleague from Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), we are justified to wonder where that association is going, what is its role? If it is simply an intermediary that will be set up to distribute federal grants to colleges and universities, then, we will have to stand against it.
I think that a statement by the hon. member for Northumberland would be in order at this time.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: I may say once again, to correct an earlier remark, that I did not say this was its first purpose or its main purpose. This is one of its many purposes. I am sorry, since this seems to have become such an enormous issue. For many years now, without any objection from that corner, the Canadian universities foundation has been performing this task. I would think the hon. member for Lapointe would know this very well. I am really shocked to discover he apparently does not realize that the new association, which is simply replacing two existing bodies, is carrying on the functions these two bodies carried on separately.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: I know what the Canadian universities foundation was doing, but it was not with the consent of the provinces involved. The province of Quebec did not give its consent but received, quite rightly, part of the federal personal income tax. The hon. member for Northumberland said that the federal government had the authority to change that. This is the point I should like to have explained. I know these per capita grants have been given in many areas and in other provinces, and I know they were given with the consent of those provinces. However, the province of Quebec remained out of that plan.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext: I am sorry if I gave the wrong impression. This does not affect the constitutional position in any way whatever. Things will continue exactly as they always have.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to ask a few questions right now. I do not know as much about this measure as the hon. member for
Lapointe does because I have not had much to do with the universities foundation. However I am always interested in an agency that appears to be operating in the public domain but remains a private agency. The hon. member has referred to the $2 per capita which is distributed, and that is a large sum of money. It amounts to something like $14 million in Ontario and $10 million in Quebec. Why should this amount be distributed by this agency? Why has the government not introduced this bill rather than leaving it to a private member? It seems to me the work of the organization falls within the public domain, especially if it is a distributing agency for the federal government. If this is the case, then the organization should get its jurisdiction from a public act.
I noticed there was a schedule attached to the bill, and I have looked at it quickly. I find none of the new universities or colleges in the list. This raises the problem, how do these new universities obtain a listing? I am interested particularly in Laurentian University and I notice it is not listed. Second, and this may be a hypothetical question, there is in Ontario a new class of college growing up. These colleges have not asked for that status as yet, nor have they been particularly concerned about it. I am referring to such schools as NOIT, the technical institute of northern Ontario, and EOIT, the eastern technical institute in Ottawa. I believe there are others, and they are somewhat on a par with Ryer-son, which has gone much beyond the normal technical school type of training. It seems to me that one of these days there is going to be a desire on the part of students, instructors and these institutions to establish them as colleges and start giving degree courses in highly technical fields. This has been done in many states in the United States. All sorts of queer sounding degrees are given by these colleges in highly technical fields.
There has been a reluctance on the part of the universities to recognize new colleges. If this is true, and it has been the case until recently, then it is going to be very difficult for any of these new technical colleges to obtain a status that would allow them to be listed in this schedule. It seems to me, from a reading of it, that we are establishing a schedule now that can be added to only by agreement of the board of directors of the conference, the persons named in the schedule. If this is so, it seems to me we are again involved in this problem of whether or not this should be a public agency or a private agency, and whether or not such a
[Mr. Gregoire.l

bill should be introduced by a cabinet minister.
There is no question about the fact that I do not understand this bill as well as some other members understand it. However, it seems to me the points that have been raised are points in which many people in Canada are interested, especially in view of the rapid changes taking place in this field, and there may be a desire to make sure these new schools are not being overlooked by the conference.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
Dealing with the hon. member's first point, once again I think it is important to emphasize that the role which the association plays in distributing the per capita grants at the request of the federal government is minor in relation to its whole role. Its whole role is comparable to many other associations. It is true it needs incorporation because of its financial responsibility, but its total purpose is far more in the private than in the public realm. If the time comes, and the hon. member suggested it might, when these roles were reversed, his argument would be very well taken; but at the moment that is not the case.
The association does a great deal of research. It provides an information service for its members. It has an awards division and an international program division. It has a great many jobs to do which, as a voluntary association of universities it is quite justified in doing, and which jobs really have nothing to do with the federal government.
On the second point with regard to the new universities, some of these at the moment are being processed, and others have already been processed. We did not amend the schedule because once they have reached the criteria set out by the association they will automatically become members. As I say, they have already done so or are in the process of doing so now.
I might add that in the bylaws of the association there is a definition of criteria it has established for membership. These include that a college or university, in each of the three years preceding its date for application, must have had a total enrolment of at least 200 members, and must satisfy a visiting committee appointed by the board of directors of the association that it is providing education of university standard.
This brings me to the third point in the hon. member's speech which I found very interesting, but again a little further afield than the actual bill before us. My impression
Private Bills
of both the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges and the C.U.F., which this association is replacing, is that there is among their number a very wide representation of the point of view that the hon. member expressed, that provided the criteria are met, particularly the two with regard to enrolment of 200 and being of university education level, as many institutions as possible should be included. But beyond that I cannot go, except to assure the hon. member that this is a matter of a great deal of concern to institutions now members of the association.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Objects.

maintopic: ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am expressing my own personal point of view, but it seems to me we should be concerning ourselves with so-called higher education, or education at the university level, as being the type of education which is necessary to foster and promote the greatest possible development in Canada. Therefore we should be looking- and I hope to heaven the government one day will do so-at the question of higher education from the point of view of having the federal parliament involved in it, participating as fully as possible and trying to promote and advance the interests of Canada rather than continuing to promote and advance the segmentation of Canada.
I put this forth purely as a personal and individual point of view, but many people are becoming vitally concerned about the question of education at the higher or university level. This is what we should be doing and, with that viewpoint in mind, I say the objectives of the association cannot be met so long as we continue to adhere to an outmoded concept of education that the fathers of confederation developed in 1867.

Private Bills

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at five
o'clock I had asked either of the ministers concerned a question based on paragraph 7, subparagraph (iv), of the report of the special joint committee. Perhaps I might read this section again:
There should be scope for further benefits under private pension plans for those in a position to afford them, and integration of private pension plans with the Canada pension plan should be a matter of consultation between employers and employees.

That is a stated opinion of the special joint committee. As the Minister of National Revenue knows, the point was made this morning by the legislative committee of the running trades brotherhoods, and as both ministers know, this is the position taken by the Canadian Labour Congress. I am wondering whether the government has given any thought to ways in which this desirable objective might be achieved.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have given a great deal of consideration to it, as members of the committee will remember. One of the first things that was raised in the discussion of the implementation of the Canada pension plan, and from various quarters, was what would happen to already existing private plans. I pointed out, as has the Prime Minister and a number of spokesmen for the government on a number of occasions, that the constitutional rights of the federal government are limited to a number of different classifications. One of these classifications, of course, relates to members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the military, and the committee has already dealt with this question. It would have to be done by way of amendment to their superannuation acts. The same is true of the civil service.
As I have pointed out a number of times to the committee and the house, a great deal of work has gone into figuring this out and dealing with the different groups which represent civil servants across the country. In addition of course there is a very large group of Canadians who are employed in federal enterprises, where the federal writ ordinarily would apply. Some of these that come quickly to mind are such enterprises as the railways, perhaps the C.B.C., perhaps the banks and other similar groups. There are many of them. I am thinking particularly of those where-say Polymer or the C.N.R. -the federal government is in a sense the qua employer.
In other cases it really does depend, I would think, on whether or not there has been a trade union agreement negotiated between employer and employee, where there has been agreement in the past as to what proportion of the total contribution is paid by the employer and what by the employee; whether it is all paid by the employee- which I think is a very rare case, if it exists at all-or by the employer.
It would seem to me that this must be left to a greater or less degree to management 20220-776
Canada Pension Plan
and labour, depending on what their previous history has been. There are a great many variations in private plans. One of the largest industrial plans in the country, in which the federal government has no jurisdiction whatsoever, is one of the automotive plant plans, where I understand the contribution is paid entirely by the employer; although, of course, in the contract between employer and employee it is a part of the fringe benefit and might be construed by many to be thus a part of the wages. There is no direct deduction from individual workers for their contribution; it is all paid by the employer. In cases where a federal entity is the employer, this may be what happens, or it may be a matter where both groups, employer and employee, share equally, as under the general law for all Canadians coming under the Canada pension plan; or indeed they might share disparately in the required contribution. However, it is not a matter with which the federal government, will have to deal qua a government; but the individual crown corporations or crown entities will deal with it in their own specific sphere according to the kind of labour relations they have had in the past. I would not think there is any jurisdiction for the federal government as such to introduce that kind of legislation here.
With regard to the C.N.R., I remember, as a former member of the railway committee for a number of years, that representatives of the railway unions approached the committee asking for an amendment which would take care of those employees who during the depression years were laid off and could not thus contribute to their pension plan. This was never the subject of any amendment to railway legislation. I think it may often have been the subject of representations made by at least private members to the C.N.R. management itself, but it did not form a part of the legislation. I would think, therefore, that this is a matter which those who are not directly employees of the federal government will deal with on an ad hoc basis in accordance with the way their employer-employee relationships have grown up for some years in the past.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I thank the minister for her statement. What she has said does relate to the precise point I was trying to make rather than to the broad question of integration. I am not at this point arguing that there should be integration or that there should be decking rather than integration, although that is the direction in which I lean. I am simply arguing that before

Canada Pension Plan
decisions are made by those who control private pension plans, as to whether or not to integrate, there should be consultation between employers and employees.
Perhaps the minister has gone as far as she can in saying that this is her view. I hope she agrees with the view expressed by the committee that this is what should be done. In the first place, the government can set an example. Perhaps we could have reassurance on this point, that in so far as the integration of the federal civil service superannuation arrangements with the Canada pension plan is concerned, this is the subject of consultation between the government, as employer, and the staff-side representatives. Another thing the government could do, of course, would be to express its opinion along the lines of the committee's report, to which I have just referred.
There is still another beneficial step which the minister might take, and that is that she might speak to her colleague the Minister of Labour about the matter. She probably knows that there is a provision in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act which makes it very difficult, in fact almost impossible, for railway employees to put the pension question on the bargaining table when they meet with management. As I say, the limitation is because of a certain section in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Amendments to that act were asked for this morning by those who appeared before the government over in the railway committee room, so I hope the minister will speak with her colleague the Minister of Labour about that matter. Because if the government shares the view which was expressed by the joint committee, that there should be consultation before integration is effected, then let us do everything we can to bring about that consultation. As I say, I am not at this point arguing either for or against integration; I am just asking for consultation and for everything that can possibly be done to bring that consultation about.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say that I thought the Minister of Finance did make this point quite clear earlier, as have spokesmen for the government repeatedly. This plan which has been devised for the integration of public service superannuation and the Canada pension plan is one which has been worked out very carefully, through consultation with the advisory committee which deals with civil service superannua-

tion and the national joint council, every step of the way. So that consultation has been the one principle which has predominated in the federal government's attitude as an employer toward integration. We still hope that this will be considered to be a sort of guiding light to show the way in which people should operate. It may not be that we have any jurisdiction to go beyond that, except to show them what we hope will be the best kind of example.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I was aware of that. I was hoping the minister would say that, and I thank her for doing so.
